faq.a: Fibrotic marrow forces hematopoiesis to occur in the spleen (extramedullary hematopoiesis), causing massive splenomegaly.
faq.q: Why does the spleen enlarge in myelofibrosis?

faq.a: Allogeneic stem‑cell transplant is the only curative therapy, but it is feasible for few patients; most receive disease‑modifying drugs.
It is contraindicated; limited data suggest teratogenic risk, so avoid in pregnant patients.

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer presents with early satiety, anemia and a 22‑cm spleen. Which diagnostic step confirms primary myelofibrosis and why? — Bone‑marrow trephine; it demonstrates grade ≥2 reticulin fibrosis and atypical megakaryocytes, distinguishing it from reactive causes.
How does the presence of a CALR mutation influence prognosis compared with JAK2‑positive disease? — CALR mutation confers a better overall survival and lower risk of leukemic transformation.

A patient on ruxolitinib develops a new fever and neutropenia. What is your next action? — Stop ruxolitinib temporarily, obtain cultures, and start broad‑spectrum antibiotics; neutropenia increases infection risk.

Explain why hydroxyurea is used only when JAK inhibitors are unavailable. — Hydroxyurea provides cytoreduction but can worsen cytopenias and does not reduce splenomegaly as effectively as JAK inhibition.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt immediate referral for possible leukemic transformation? — Sudden increase in peripheral blasts or a rise in white‑cell count with >20 % blasts on peripheral smear.

Distinguish primary myelofibrosis from visceral leishmaniasis in a patient with splenomegaly and anemia. — Leishmaniasis shows fever, positive rK39 or bone‑marrow amastigotes, and lacks marrow fibrosis or JAK mutations.
Why is vaccination against encapsulated bacteria recommended in myelofibrosis? — Functional asplenia from splenic fibrosis impairs clearance of encapsulated organisms, raising infection risk.
What is the role of the Dynamic International Prognostic Scoring System (DIPSS‑plus) in management? — It stratifies patients into risk groups guiding intensity of therapy and transplant referral.
ai.title: Primary Myelofibrosis
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Primary myelofibrosis is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm causing marrow fibrosis, extramedullary hematopoiesis and massive splenomegaly. Diagnosis relies on bone‑marrow histology and molecular markers; prognosis follows the Dynamic International Prognostic Scoring System.

b: Bone‑marrow biopsy: grade 2–3 reticulin fibrosis, atypical megakaryocytes, and <5% blasts.
Molecular: JAK2 V617F (≈50‑60%), CALR or MPL mutations in JAK‑negative cases.
sections.p: A chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm in which abnormal megakaryocytes release cytokines that stimulate reticulin and collagen deposition in the marrow, leading to cytopenias and extramedullary hematopoiesis.

t.b: Confirms fibrosis and rules out other marrow failures; presence of grade ≥2 reticulin supports diagnosis.
Identifies driver mutation; a positive result strengthens diagnosis and guides therapy.
Looks for leukoerythroblastosis, teardrop RBCs, and nucleated RBCs; supports extramedullary hematopoiesis.

b: Age >65 yr, hemoglobin <10 g/dL, leukocyte count >25 ×10⁹/L, circulating blasts ≥2%, platelet count <100 ×10⁹/L, constitutional symptoms, and unfavorable karyotype each add 1 point.
Low (0), intermediate‑1 (1‑2), intermediate‑2 (3‑4), high (≥5) risk.
sections.p: Prognosis is stratified by the Dynamic International Prognostic Scoring System (DIPSS‑plus).

b: Primary clonal disease (JAK2, CALR, MPL).
Secondary to chronic infections: HIV, TB, malaria (rare but reported).
Drug‑induced: hydroxyurea, alkylating agents.
Post‑polycythemia vera or essential thrombocythemia transformation.
sections.p: Primary (idiopathic) myelofibrosis is the commonest; secondary fibrosis can follow other marrow disorders or chronic infections prevalent in low‑resource settings.

b: Fatigue, night sweats, weight loss.
Early satiety, abdominal fullness from splenomegaly.
Anemia‑related dyspnea; occasional bleeding from thrombocytopenia.
Leukoerythroblastosis on smear (teardrop RBCs, nucleated RBCs).
sections.p: Patients often present with constitutional symptoms and a massive, often painful, splenomegaly.

b: CBC with differential – looks for anemia, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia.
Peripheral smear – teardrop RBCs, nucleated RBCs, immature granulocytes.
Ultrasound or bedside palpation – estimates spleen size when CT unavailable.
sections.p: Focus on confirming fibrosis, assessing mutation status, and evaluating disease burden while considering test availability.

t.b: Quantifies cytopenias; severe anemia (<10 g/dL) or thrombocytopenia (<100 ×10⁹/L) signals higher risk.
Detects leukoerythroblastosis; teardrop cells suggest marrow fibrosis.
Measures splenic dimensions; massive splenomegaly (>20 cm) supports extramedullary hematopoiesis.
Provides definitive fibrosis grade; if unavailable, rely on clinical picture and smear.
Use referral lab; if not possible, treat based on clinical criteria.

b: Transformation to acute myeloid leukemia (≥20 % blasts).
Severe anemia causing cardiac decompensation.
Massive splenic infarction or rupture.
Infections due to neutropenia or functional asplenia.
sections.p: Complications can be rapidly fatal and require urgent attention.

b: JAK1/2 inhibitor (ruxolitinib) – first‑line for symptomatic splenomegaly or constitutional symptoms; avoids cytotoxicity of chemotherapy.
Hydroxyurea – cytoreduction when JAK inhibitor unavailable; monitor for cytopenias.
Supportive care: red‑cell transfusion for symptomatic anemia, platelet transfusion if bleeding, iron chelation if transfusion‑related overload.
Allogeneic stem‑cell transplant – only curative option, limited to eligible young patients.
sections.p: Therapy aims to control symptoms, reduce splenomegaly, and modify disease biology.

b: CBC every 4–6 weeks while on therapy; more frequent if cytopenias develop.
Physical exam for spleen size at each visit.
Annual bone‑marrow assessment if disease status changes.
Vaccinate against encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, meningococcus) because of functional asplenia.
sections.p: Regular monitoring detects progression and treatment toxicity.

b: Secondary myelofibrosis from chronic myeloid leukemia – CML shows BCR‑ABL1 positivity and higher leukocyte counts.
Visceral leishmaniasis – endemic in East Africa, presents with fever, hepatosplenomegaly, but lacks marrow fibrosis and JAK mutations.
Thalassaemia major – severe anemia and extramedullary hematopoiesis, but microcytosis and target cells dominate smear.
sections.p: Conditions that also cause massive splenomegaly and leukoerythroblastosis.

b: Normal leukocyte count does not exclude disease; fibrosis can be present with leukopenia.
Mild reticulin fibrosis on biopsy can be seen in early disease or reactive states; correlate clinically.
JAK2‑negative cases may still be primary myelofibrosis if CALR or MPL mutations are present.
sections.p: Certain findings may be falsely reassuring or confusing.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden splenic rupture or acute abdomen
Rapid rise in blasts suggesting leukemic transformation
Severe anemia with cardiac failure signs
